name: Kasai Procedure (Hepatic Portoenterostomy)
overview: Roux-en-Y hepatic portoenterostomy for biliary atresia

pimpingQuestions.question: What are the two proposed embryologic theories for biliary atresia?
pimpingQuestions.answer: 1) Defective ductal plate remodeling (embryonic form, 15%, associated with laterality defects/polysplenia), 2) Perinatal viral infection (reovirus, CMV) triggering autoimmune bile duct destruction. Most evidence supports genetic susceptibility plus perinatal viral trigger.

pimpingQuestions.question: At what level is the transection made in Kasai, and what guides the plane?
pimpingQuestions.answer: Flush with the liver capsule at the porta hepatis bifurcation plate. Microscopic bile ductules (<150 micrometers) within this fibrous plate communicate with intrahepatic ducts and drain into the Roux limb. The transection must be precisely at the liver surface — too shallow misses the ductules, too deep injures portal structures.

pimpingQuestions.question: What structures immediately posterior to the bile duct remnant must be preserved during Kasai?
pimpingQuestions.answer: The portal vein bifurcation and hepatic artery branches (right and left). These run directly behind the fibrous remnant. Injury to either is catastrophic and may preclude future liver transplantation.

pimpingQuestions.question: What is the critical timing window for Kasai, and what are success rates by age?
pimpingQuestions.answer: Must be performed before 60-90 days of age. Bile clearance rates: <30 days: 70-80%, 30-60 days: 50-60%, 60-90 days: 25-40%, >90 days: <20%. Even after successful Kasai, 50% need liver transplant by age 5 and 70% by age 20.

pimpingQuestions.question: What unique complication occurs in 40-50% of post-Kasai patients?
pimpingQuestions.answer: Ascending cholangitis — enteric bacteria ascend the Roux limb into intrahepatic bile ducts. Treated with IV antibiotics (gram-negative and anaerobic coverage). Prophylactic TMP-SMX is given for 1-2 years. Recurrent cholangitis accelerates hepatic fibrosis and hastens need for transplantation.
